So, you're saying you agree with all of it?  I don't.  I agree with most of
it but there are key points that I reject.

Kaczynski claims we have to experience disaster on a mass scale before we
can correct our course.  This is more in line with Christian eschatology
than my secular eschatology.

FWIW, here's something I wrote in Dec. of 99.

I disagreed with 19 of the 232 points at

http://www.unabombertrial.com/manifesto/index.html


Here are the ones I disagree with: 1, 4, 96, 100, 109, 111, 117, 124, 125,
130,
131, 166, 193, 196, 200, 204, 206, 214, and 218.


1
-----
Disagree.  The Industrial Revolution has had a mixture of consequences--some
good some bad.  Rather that "disasterous," I would describe it as hazardous
and
challenging.  The continued development of technology will not necessarily
"worsen the situation."  Unbridled technology probably *would* worsen the
situation.  However, the challenge is to control the developmnet and
deployment
of technology wisely. There is no assurance we will be able to do this
wisely,
but there is no reason we can't.

2
-----
Mostly agree.  If "the system" is understood to include the set of attitudes
and beliefs that now predominate, then it is probably true that the human
condition will inevitably worsen as long as the system survives.  We can't
preclude the possibility, however, that certain predominant beliefs and
attitudes could change.

3
----
Mostly agree.  This is a tricky statement however.  "If" is the key word.
What
evidence is there that this is likely?  If the plane crashes on which I am
travelling, the consequences will no doubt be painful--likely fatal.  So,
this
might be true but without some sense of the likelihood, it is not very
maningful and not likely to cause me to change my travel plans.  In the
context
of the manifesto, it's clear that the author means to say that breakdown is
very likely (almost certain) and uses this "true" statement to conclude
(given
in the next paragraph, 5, that revolution is the appropriate course of
action)

     If we had never done anything violent and had
     submitted the present writings to a publisher,
     they probably would not have been accepted.
     If they had been been accepted and published,
     they probably would not have attracted many
     readers, because it's more fun to watch the
     entertainment put out by the media than to read
     a sober essay. Even if these writings had had
     many readers, most of these readers would soon
     have forgotten what they had read as their
     minds were flooded by the mass of material to
     which the media expose them. In order to get
     our message before the public with some chance
     of making a lasting impression, we've had to kill
     people.

Many dismiss the words from the terrorist because they come from the
terrorist.
 The Unabomber probably could have done better through conventional
publishing
channels, and later, through the Internet (he does mention the Internet here
but the Internet was just developing during the Unabomber's rampage).

In any case, this document was not worth killing anybody for.
